content_voiceover: Here's a high-yield association: blood type O is linked to the lowest plasma levels of von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII compared to non-O blood types. The Shima 1995 data, broken down by ABO genotype, shows OO individuals averaging around 81 IU per deciliter of vWF, compared to roughly 113 to 115 for AA, BB, and AB genotypes, a statistically significant difference. The FVIII table below pools five independent studies, and in every single one, group O consistently shows the lowest Factor VIII coagulant activity relative to A, B, and AB groups. The proposed mechanism relates to increased plasma clearance of vWF, thought to be mediated by ABO-dependent glycosylation effects on vWF's clearance receptors. Why does this matter clinically? Because normal vWF and FVIII levels run roughly 25 to 30% lower in type O individuals, relying on population-wide reference ranges can lead to overdiagnosis of von Willebrand disease in type O patients, and potential underdiagnosis in non-O patients. Boards love testing this ABO-vWF association.
keypoints: Blood type O has the lowest vWF and FVIII levels of all ABO types
Non-O individuals average ~25-30% higher vWF/FVIII than type O
Clinical pitfall: standard cutoffs risk overdiagnosing vWD in type O patients
Consistent finding replicated across multiple independent cohort studies
keypoint_voiceover: Key fact: blood type O carries the lowest plasma vWF and Factor VIII levels of any ABO type, consistently shown across multiple studies. Non-O individuals run about 25 to 30% higher. Clinically, this means population reference ranges can overdiagnose von Willebrand disease in type O patients, so interpret vWF and FVIII results with ABO type in mind.
